note: Curated 'spicy' (adult-humor) fun facts, grounded in verified history. Used only when spice='spicy'. Keys are matched loosely (case, punctuation and 'City, ST' suffixes are ignored). Add your own entries following the same shape.

entries.name: Las Vegas, Nevada
facts: The Strip isn't actually in Las Vegas — it sits in unincorporated Paradise, Nevada. The name was not a coincidence.
Prostitution is illegal in Clark County, which is exactly why Nevada's legal brothels huddle just outside city limits. Supply and demand is a beautiful thing.
Bugsy Siegel built the Flamingo with mob money, opened it in 1946, and got shot dead in 1947. One star, would not visit again.
You can get married in a Vegas drive-thru without leaving the truck. Commitment issues, solved.

entries.name: Reno, Nevada
facts: Reno was America's quickie-divorce capital — in the 1900s you could end a marriage with a six-week stay. The original easy-out.
Reno calls itself the Biggest Little City in the World, which sounds like a personal problem.
Nevada's brothels are only legal outside city limits, so Reno is a short drive from a very different kind of rest stop.

entries.name: Pahrump, Nevada
facts: The Chicken Ranch, a legal brothel opened in 1976, sits just outside Pahrump — the closest legal 'hospitality' to Las Vegas.
In 1978 the Chicken Ranch burned down in a suspected arson — and reopened from trailers five days later. Motivated.

entries.name: New Orleans, Louisiana
facts: Storyville was America's only legal red-light district, running 1897–1917 until the Navy shut it down in WWI. Sailors: ruining fun since forever.
Storyville even printed 'blue books' — guidebooks to the brothels with prices, services, and 'stock.' Yelp, 1905 edition.

entries.name: Butte, Montana
facts: Butte's Dumas Brothel ran from 1890 to 1982 — the longest in U.S. history. Customer loyalty, achieved.
The Dumas' last madam shot her husband in a bar in 1959, served nine months, then went right back to running the place.

entries.name: Wallace, Idaho
facts: Wallace, Idaho ran brothels openly until 1991 — one is now a museum, and you can rent a former brothel on Airbnb.
Wallace hid its brothels in plain sight for over a century. Subtlety was not their strong suit.

entries.name: Tombstone, Arizona
facts: The O.K. Corral gunfight lasted about 30 seconds. Tombstone has been milking it for 140 years.

entries.name: Deadwood, South Dakota
facts: Wild Bill Hickok was shot dead in Deadwood holding aces and eights — the 'dead man's hand.' Literally a losing hand.
Deadwood's saloons, gambling, and brothels made it the wildest boomtown of the Black Hills gold rush.

entries.name: Fort Worth, Texas
facts: Hell's Half Acre was Fort Worth's official red-light district from the 1870s — saloons, gambling dens and brothels built for trail-weary cowboys.
By 1907 the Acre had dozens of 'crib' shacks selling sex for pocket change, plus a gunfight between gambler Luke Short and marshal Jim Courtright.
The city demolished Hell's Half Acre twice, but it always grew back until the brothels were finally cleared in the early 1900s.

entries.name: Dodge City, Kansas
facts: Dodge City's Front Street packed saloons, gambling halls and brothels to serve cowboys fresh off the cattle trail — the 'Queen of the Cowtowns.'
Between 1877 and 1886 Dodge City was one of the most dangerous towns in America, where gunfights were just the evening entertainment.

entries.name: Fresno, California
facts: Fresno's Chinatown was once a red-light district — its underground tunnels and basements hid gambling and prostitution for decades.
Chinese immigrants who built the railroad were pushed west of the tracks into Chinatown, where the vice trade thrived.

entries.name: Milford, Pennsylvania
facts: Gambino crime boss John Gotti kept a hilltop estate in Milford — the Pennsylvania Crime Commission said he entertained mob associates there.
Gotti's $300,000 Milford Heights estate was bought in 1988 through his son and son-in-law, per Pike County deed records.
Milford's Columns Museum holds the 'Lincoln Flag' — the blood-stained flag from Lincoln's Ford's Theatre box, used to cushion his head after he was shot.

entries.name: Lords Valley, Pennsylvania
facts: Lords Valley sits in the Pocono honeymoon belt: Cove Haven's Morris Wilkins invented the heart-shaped bathtub in 1963, making the Poconos the 'Honeymoon Capital of the World.'
The Poconos' seven-foot 'champagne glass' whirlpool for two debuted at Cove Haven in 1983 — couples climbed a staircase to soak in a giant acrylic flute.

entries.name: Lakeville, Pennsylvania
facts: Cove Haven's Morris Wilkins invented the heart-shaped bathtub in 1963, turning Lakeville and the Poconos into the 'Honeymoon Capital of the World.'
Cove Haven topped the tub with a seven-foot champagne-glass whirlpool for two in 1983 — couples climbed a staircase to get in.

entries.name: Girard, Ohio
facts: Girard's Past Times Arcade runs 600-plus pinball machines and video games, nearly all playable for $20 a day in a former grocery store.
Owner Rob Berk holds the Guinness World Record for the largest pinball collection on Earth: 1,041 machines, documented in 2024.
The Henry Barnhisel House, a Greek Revival built about 1840, is on the National Register and may have sheltered Underground Railroad travellers.
Girard's 1993 boys' basketball state title is still the only one ever won by a Trumbull County school.
Four men bought Solomon Kline's land in 1836 to found Girard; the Black Horse Tavern became the town's first post office.
Suffragist Elizabeth Hauser was born in Girard in 1873 and edited the Girard Grit before working for the national suffrage campaign.

entries.name: Indian Lake, Ohio
facts: Indian Lake was built in the 1850s as the Lewistown Reservoir, dug by Irish laborers to feed the Miami and Erie Canal.
The canal went obsolete within years, but the lake stayed — and at 5,104 acres it's the second largest inland lake in Ohio.
Sandy Beach Amusement Park opened in 1924 billed as the 'Midwest's Million Dollar Playground' and the 'Atlantic City of the West'.
Its 2,000-foot wooden roller coaster went by four names over the years: Coaster, Thriller, Big Dipper and Silver Streak.
The Minnewawa Dance Hall hosted Paul Whiteman and Rudy Vallee, and its 1931 endurance dance marathon ran 80 days and 2 hours.
A July 4, 1961 brawl involving nearly 500 youths kicked off almost a decade of Independence Day riots at Russells Point.
Cedar Point and Kings Island finished it: the park closed in 1975 and was razed in 1982, leaving one re-lit 1920s bridge.
Local lore claims an abandoned lead mine sits under the lake, and that Chicago mobsters once used the old dancehall.
The lake's spillway is where the Great Miami River begins, and its saugeye fishing is known nationally.
Over 100,000 people turned up at Indian Lake for the 1953 Ohio Sesquicentennial celebration.

entries.name: Cuba, Missouri
facts: Four miles west of Cuba on Route 66 stands the Red Rocker, 42 feet high and for a time the world's largest rocking chair.
Cuba was Missouri's biggest apple town from 1895 to 1920 — 'The Land of the Big Red Apple' — and the barrels kept it rolling.
Bette Davis and Amelia Earhart both passed through Cuba, and both are painted into the town's Viva Cuba murals.
Cuba is the official Route 66 Mural City, named so by the Missouri legislature for its twelve outdoor murals.
The Wagon Wheel Motel, with its original guest cottages, has been taking Route 66 travellers since the 1930s.
Cuba was platted in 1857 once it was certain the railroad was coming, and named after the island of Cuba.
President Harry S. Truman stopped in Cuba on a Route 66 tour and surveyed the land that became Indian Hills Lake.
Cuba was the site of Missouri's first Adopt a Highway program.
